name: Doji
definition: A single-candlestick formation in which the open and close are equal or virtually equal, producing a very small or nonexistent real body. In technical analysis it is read as a sign of indecision between buyers and sellers; as with all candlestick patterns, it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictive law.
intuition: Buyers and sellers fought to a draw during the period: price traveled up and down but ended essentially where it started, so neither side is in control.
mechanics: Computed directly from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is at or near zero relative to the period's range (a common convention classifies a candle as a doji when the body is no more than a few percent of the high-low range). The position of the open/close within the range defines subtypes (long-legged, dragonfly, gravestone).
formula: Doji when |C - O| <= epsilon * (H - L), where O, H, L, C are the period's open, high, low, close and epsilon is a small threshold (often ~0.05).
failure_modes: A lone doji is a neutral indicator with little information content; it appears frequently in sideways markets where it says nothing about direction. Reversal interpretations often fail without confirmation from the next candle or other indicators.
misconceptions: A doji does not by itself signal a reversal; it signals indecision, and the prevailing trend can just as easily continue. It is also not rare in the absolute sense on low-liquidity or very short timeframes.
example: A stock rallies for a week, then prints a daily candle that opens at 50.10 and closes at 50.12 with a high of 51.00 and low of 49.20. Analysts read the doji as waning buying momentum and wait for a bearish confirmation candle before treating it as a reversal warning.

name: Long-legged doji
definition: A doji variant with long upper and lower shadows and open and close at or near the same price, typically near the middle of the period's range. It is interpreted in technical analysis as strong two-sided pressure ending in a standoff, often read as a sign that the prior trend is losing conviction.
intuition: Price was pushed far up and far down during the period, but neither side could hold its gains; the market ended exactly where it began after a wide-ranging battle.
mechanics: Identified from OHLC data as a candle with a near-zero real body (open approximately equal to close) whose upper and lower shadows are both long relative to the body and typically to recent candles. No strict numerical threshold is canonical; charting packages apply their own body/range rules.
failure_modes: It only shows indecision, not direction; in choppy or low-volume markets long-legged dojis are common and meaningless. Treating it as a standalone reversal signal produces frequent false positives.
misconceptions: It is not inherently bearish or bullish; its meaning depends entirely on the preceding trend and on confirmation from subsequent candles.
example: After a two-week uptrend, a stock opens at 100, trades between 95 and 105, and closes at 100.05. The long-legged doji marks exhaustion of both sides; traders watch the next session to see which way the stalemate resolves.

name: Dragonfly doji
definition: A doji variant in which the open, high, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long lower shadow and little or no upper shadow (a T shape). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod selling that was fully absorbed by buyers, and treat it as a possible bullish reversal sign when it appears after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
intuition: Sellers drove price sharply lower during the period, but buyers pushed it all the way back to the opening level, showing demand underneath the market.
mechanics: From OHLC data: open, high, and close cluster at or near the same price (small tolerance), while the low sits far below, so the lower shadow dominates the range. It is the single-candle mirror of the gravestone doji.
failure_modes: Its reversal implication fails often in strong downtrends, where the bounce back to the open is only temporary short covering. In quiet markets it occurs frequently and carries no signal.
misconceptions: A dragonfly doji is not automatically bullish; after an advance it can mark exhaustion instead. It requires confirmation from the following candle before it supports any directional hypothesis.
example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 40.00, falls to 37.50 intraday, then recovers to close at 40.00. The resulting dragonfly doji suggests sellers failed to hold the lows, and traders watch for a higher close the next day as confirmation.

name: Gravestone doji
definition: A doji variant in which the open, low, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long upper shadow and little or no lower shadow (an inverted T). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod buying that was fully rejected by sellers, and treat it as a possible bearish reversal sign when it appears after an advance; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
intuition: Buyers drove price sharply higher during the period, but sellers forced it all the way back down to the opening level, showing supply sitting above the market.
mechanics: From OHLC data: open, low, and close cluster at or near the same price (small tolerance), while the high sits far above, so the upper shadow dominates the range. It is the single-candle mirror of the dragonfly doji.
failure_modes: In strong uptrends the rejection is often temporary profit-taking and the trend resumes, so reversal readings fail. It is also common and meaningless in flat, low-volume sessions.
misconceptions: A gravestone doji is not automatically a sell signal; after a decline it can instead mark seller exhaustion. It needs bearish confirmation from the next candle.
example: After a rally, a stock opens at 60.00, spikes to 63.00, and is sold back down to close at 60.00. The gravestone doji shows the highs were rejected; traders look for a lower close the following session before acting on a bearish reading.

name: Spinning top
definition: A single candlestick with a small real body vertically centered between upper and lower shadows that are both noticeably longer than the body. Like the doji, it is read as indecision between buyers and sellers and is treated in technical analysis as a possible sign of trend exhaustion when it follows an extended move; it is a hypothesis requiring confirmation, not a predictive law.
intuition: Both bulls and bears pushed price around during the period, but neither could keep it anywhere; the close near the open shows the tug-of-war ended in a draw.
mechanics: Identified from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is small relative to the total range (larger than a doji's near-zero body; a common convention allows up to roughly 5% of the range before calling it a doji instead), with meaningful shadows on both sides. The close may be above or below the open.
failure_modes: Spinning tops are extremely common, so most occurrences are inconsequential, especially within ranges. Even after extended trends, many spinning tops are followed by continuation rather than reversal.
misconceptions: A spinning top does not predict a reversal on its own; the following candle must confirm. It is also not the same as a doji: its body is small but visible.
example: After a long advance, a stock opens at 80.00, trades between 78.50 and 81.50, and closes at 80.20. The spinning top hints that buyers are losing control; a strong down candle the next day would confirm a reversal reading.

name: Marubozu
definition: A long-bodied candlestick with no (or almost no) shadows, so that the open and close coincide with the period's extreme prices: a white/green marubozu opens at the low and closes at the high, and a black/red marubozu opens at the high and closes at the low. It is read as one-sided dominance throughout the period and is usually interpreted as a continuation signal.
intuition: One side controlled the entire session from the first trade to the last: buyers never let price dip below the open (bullish marubozu) or sellers never let it rise above the open (bearish marubozu).
mechanics: From OHLC data: the real body spans essentially the full high-low range, with upper and lower shadows at or near zero. Partial variants exist: an opening marubozu lacks a shadow only at the open side, a closing marubozu only at the close side.
failure_modes: A single marubozu late in an extended move can mark exhaustion (a climactic final push) rather than continuation. On very short timeframes or illiquid instruments, shadowless candles occur routinely and carry little information.
misconceptions: It is not a guarantee the trend continues; context matters, and a marubozu into strong resistance or support often precedes a pullback rather than immediate follow-through.
example: A stock opens at 25.00, its session low, and grinds upward all day to close at 26.40, its session high. This white marubozu shows uninterrupted buying pressure and is read as supporting continuation of the advance.

name: Hammer
definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the period's range, a long lower shadow (conventionally at least twice the body length), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal because sellers drove price down but buyers recovered nearly all of the loss; it is a hypothesis that requires confirmation.
intuition: Sellers smashed price down during the period, but buyers hammered it back up to close near the open, showing the decline was rejected.
mechanics: From OHLC data: the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is very small, and the body sits near the high. The identical shape after an uptrend is called a hanging man; trend context, not shape, distinguishes them.
formula: Hammer heuristic: (min(O, C) - L) >= 2 * |C - O| and (H - max(O, C)) <= |C - O|, after a downtrend.
failure_modes: In a strong downtrend a hammer is often just a pause before further declines, so unconfirmed long entries fail frequently. Its reliability also drops on low volume or away from support levels.
misconceptions: The body color is not decisive (a green close is modestly stronger, but a red hammer is still a hammer), and the shape alone is not the pattern: without a preceding downtrend it is not a hammer.
example: After a month-long slide, a stock opens at 30.00, falls to 27.50, then rallies to close at 29.90. The next day a strong white candle closes above 30.50, confirming the hammer and prompting reversal-focused traders to go long with a stop below 27.50.

name: Hanging man
definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the range, a long lower shadow (conventionally two or more times the body), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after an uptrend. It has the same shape as a hammer; technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal warning because the deep intraperiod selloff revealed latent selling pressure, though the reading requires bearish confirmation.
intuition: Price was dumped hard during the session and only partly recovered; the fact that sellers could push it that low at all, after a long rise, is taken as a crack in the uptrend.
mechanics: From OHLC data: identical geometry to the hammer (small body near the high, lower shadow >= ~2x body, minimal upper shadow); the distinguishing feature is context, since it must follow an advance. Confirmation is typically a lower close on the following candle.
failure_modes: The recovery to near the open shows buyers are still active, so many hanging men are followed by further gains; acting short without confirmation has a high failure rate. In strong trends it repeatedly fails as a topping signal.
misconceptions: The shape alone does not make a hanging man: the same candle after a decline is a hammer, a bullish sign. Nor is a hanging man an immediate sell signal; it is a warning that needs a confirming down candle.
example: After a steady six-week climb, a stock opens at 70.00, plunges to 66.00 intraday, and closes at 69.80. Chartists flag the hanging man and wait; a close below 68.50 the next day would confirm the bearish reading.

name: Inverted hammer
definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal: buyers mounted an intraperiod rally that sellers could not fully erase, hinting that demand is emerging; confirmation by a higher close next period is normally required.
intuition: In a falling market, buyers finally staged a real push upward during the session; even though it was sold back toward the open, the attempt shows bulls are waking up.
mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is very small, and the body sits near the low, after a preceding decline. The same shape after an uptrend is a shooting star.
failure_modes: Because it closes near its low, the inverted hammer by itself still shows sellers winning the session, and downtrends often continue. Without bullish confirmation it is one of the weaker single-candle reversal candidates.
misconceptions: It is not a shooting star: the two have identical geometry but opposite context and meaning. And it is not a buy signal on its own; the standard use requires the next candle to close higher.
example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 15.00, spikes to 16.20, and settles back to close at 15.05. A close above 15.50 the next session would be taken as confirmation that the inverted hammer marked a bottoming attempt.

name: Shooting star
definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal signal: buyers drove price sharply higher intraperiod but sellers forced it back near the open, showing the rally was rejected; it is a hypothesis that needs confirmation.
intuition: The market shot up during the session but fell back to earth before the close, leaving a long tail that shows buyers could not hold the highs.
mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow is at least about twice the real body, the lower shadow is minimal, and the body sits near the period's low, after a preceding advance. Its geometry is identical to the inverted hammer; the uptrend context is what makes it a shooting star.
failure_modes: In strong bull trends shooting stars frequently mark only brief pauses before new highs. A close near the high of the next candle negates the pattern entirely.
misconceptions: A shooting star is not confirmed bearish until the next candle closes lower; the pattern alone shows rejection, not a completed reversal. It also cannot exist without a preceding uptrend.
example: After a two-week rally, a stock opens at 90.00, surges to 94.00, and closes at 90.20. Traders flag the shooting star and treat a close below 89.00 the next day as confirmation of a downside reversal.

name: Bullish engulfing
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small black (down) body is followed by a larger white (up) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major bottom reversal signal because buyers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor.
intuition: After a falling session, buyers arrived with enough force to open lower and close above where the previous session opened, swallowing the sellers' progress whole.
mechanics: From OHLC data: C1 < O1 (down candle), then O2 < C1 and C2 > O1, so the second real body engulfs the first. Engulfing is defined on bodies, not shadows (when the full high-low range is engulfed it is an outside bar). Confirmation is sought in follow-through buying on the next candle.
formula: Bullish engulfing when C1 < O1, C2 > O2, O2 <= C1, C2 >= O1 (bodies strictly compared per convention).
failure_modes: In persistent downtrends many bullish engulfing patterns mark only one-day short-covering bounces before new lows. Signals formed in choppy, range-bound markets are especially unreliable.
misconceptions: The shadows do not need to be engulfed; only the real bodies matter for the classic definition. It is also not a standalone buy signal; practitioners typically demand confirmation or confluence with support.
example: A stock in a downtrend closes at 48.00 after opening at 49.00; the next day it opens at 47.50 and closes at 49.50. The white body engulfs the prior black body, and traders watch for follow-through above 49.50 as confirmation.

name: Bearish engulfing
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small white (up) body is followed by a larger black (down) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major top reversal signal because sellers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor.
intuition: After a rising session, sellers hit the market hard enough to open higher and close below where the previous session opened, erasing the buyers' progress in one move.
mechanics: From OHLC data: C1 > O1 (up candle), then O2 > C1 and C2 < O1, so the second real body engulfs the first. Only the bodies must overlap; shadow containment is not required. Follow-through weakness on the next candle is used as confirmation.
formula: Bearish engulfing when C1 > O1, C2 < O2, O2 >= C1, C2 <= O1 (bodies strictly compared per convention).
failure_modes: In strong bull markets bearish engulfing patterns often mark one-day profit-taking before the advance resumes. They are also common noise in sideways ranges where neither direction follows through.
misconceptions: The pattern does not require the second candle's shadows to engulf the first candle's range. And it is not an automatic short signal; context (resistance, volume, prior trend maturity) and confirmation matter.
example: A stock in an uptrend closes at 55.00 after opening at 54.00; the next day it opens at 55.50 and closes at 53.50. The black body engulfs the prior white body, and a lower close the following day would confirm the bearish reading.

name: Piercing line
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in a downtrend: a long black candle is followed by a white candle that opens below the prior low (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway up into the prior black body. Technical analysts read it as a potential bottom reversal signal, a weaker cousin of the bullish engulfing pattern.
intuition: Sellers gapped the market down at the open, but buyers drove price back up through more than half of the previous session's losses, piercing deep into their territory.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 opens at or below L1 and closes above the midpoint (O1 + C1) / 2 of the first body but below O1 (otherwise it would be a bullish engulfing). The deeper the close into the first body, the stronger the conventional reading.
formula: Piercing line when C1 < O1, O2 <= L1, and (O1 + C1)/2 < C2 < O1.
failure_modes: A close that only just passes the midpoint is weak and often fails, especially in strong downtrends. On 24-hour markets like forex where gaps are rare, the opening-gap requirement is often relaxed, which dilutes the pattern.
misconceptions: Closing above the prior candle's high or open turns it into an engulfing pattern, not a piercing line; the close must stop within the first body. It is also not a confirmed reversal without follow-through.
example: A stock falls, printing a candle from 44.00 open to 42.00 close (low 41.80). The next day opens at 41.50 and closes at 43.50, above the 43.00 midpoint of the prior body: a piercing line that bulls read as a bottoming attempt.

name: Dark cloud cover
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in an uptrend: a long white candle is followed by a black candle that opens above the prior high (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway down into the prior white body. Technical analysts read it as a potential top reversal signal, the bearish mirror of the piercing line and a weaker cousin of the bearish engulfing pattern.
intuition: Buyers gapped the market up at the open, but sellers dragged price back down through more than half of the previous session's gains, casting a dark cloud over the rally.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candle 2 opens at or above H1 and closes below the midpoint (O1 + C1) / 2 of the first body but above O1 (otherwise it would be a bearish engulfing). Deeper penetration of the first body strengthens the conventional bearish reading.
formula: Dark cloud cover when C1 > O1, O2 >= H1, and O1 < C2 < (O1 + C1)/2.
failure_modes: Shallow penetration (barely past the midpoint) frequently fails, particularly in strong uptrends where the dip is bought. In gapless 24-hour markets the opening-gap condition is usually relaxed, weakening selectivity.
misconceptions: If the second candle closes below the first candle's open, the pattern is a bearish engulfing, not dark cloud cover. The name refers only to the partial-penetration configuration, and confirmation is still required.
example: A stock rises, printing a candle from 60.00 open to 62.00 close (high 62.20). The next day opens at 62.50 and closes at 60.50, below the 61.00 midpoint of the prior body: dark cloud cover, read as a warning of an impending top.

name: Morning star
definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps below the first body, and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major bottom reversal signal marking a shift from selling to indecision to buying.
intuition: Sellers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle, then buyers take over and recover most of the lost ground, like dawn after a dark night.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body in a downtrend; candle 2 has a small real body (ideally gapping below body 1); candle 3 is a long white body closing above the midpoint of body 1. The gap between bodies 1 and 2 (and ideally between 2 and 3) is the classic requirement, often relaxed in gap-poor markets.
failure_modes: In gapless markets (spot forex, crypto) the pattern is frequently identified without true gaps, which weakens it. A weak third candle that fails to close deep into the first body often precedes renewed decline.
misconceptions: The star need not be a doji; any small body qualifies (when it is a doji the pattern is specifically a morning doji star). The pattern is also not complete, and not actionable by convention, until the third candle closes.
example: A stock slides, printing a long black candle (52.00 to 50.00), then a tiny-bodied candle around 49.60-49.80, then a long white candle closing at 51.50, deep into the first body. Chartists read the morning star as a bottom reversal signal.

name: Evening star
definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps above the first body, and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major top reversal signal marking a shift from buying to indecision to selling; it is the bearish mirror of the morning star.
intuition: Buyers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle near the highs, then sellers seize control and erase much of the advance, like nightfall after a bright day.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body in an uptrend; candle 2 has a small real body (ideally gapping above body 1); candle 3 is a long black body closing below the midpoint of body 1. Classic definitions want gaps around the star; these are commonly relaxed in gap-poor markets.
failure_modes: In strong bull trends the third candle's dip is often bought, and the uptrend resumes. In 24-hour markets without gaps, loosely matched 'evening stars' generate many false tops.
misconceptions: The star candle can be either color and need not be a doji (a doji star makes it an evening doji star). The signal is only conventionally valid once the third candle has closed deep into the first body.
example: A stock climbs, printing a long white candle (70.00 to 72.00), then a tiny-bodied candle around 72.30-72.50, then a long black candle closing at 70.50. The evening star is read as a top reversal warning.

name: Morning doji star
definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a doji that gaps below it (the doji star), and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the morning star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger reversal signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in selling.
intuition: After heavy selling, the market opens lower but goes absolutely nowhere (a doji), then buyers storm back and reclaim most of the decline; the dead-flat middle candle shows sellers are spent.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body in a downtrend; candle 2 is a doji whose body (and classically whose range) sits below body 1; candle 3 is a long white body closing above the midpoint of body 1. When the doji also gaps away from both neighbors' shadows, the pattern becomes the rarer bullish abandoned baby.
failure_modes: True gap-separated doji stars are rare in 24-hour markets, so relaxed versions are common and less reliable. Even textbook instances fail when the broader downtrend is powerful and the third candle lacks volume.
misconceptions: It is not interchangeable with the plain morning star; the middle candle must be a doji. It is also distinct from the bullish abandoned baby, which additionally requires the doji's shadows to gap clear of both neighbors.
example: A stock falls with a long black candle (35.00 to 33.00), then prints a doji near 32.60 after gapping down, then rallies on a long white candle closing at 34.50. The morning doji star is read as a strong bottom reversal signal.

name: Evening doji star
definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a doji that gaps above it (the doji star), and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the evening star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger bearish signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in buying.
intuition: After heavy buying, the market gaps up but freezes dead flat (a doji), then sellers drive price deep back into the prior gains; the motionless middle candle shows buyers are exhausted.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body in an uptrend; candle 2 is a doji whose body (and classically whose range) sits above body 1; candle 3 is a long black body closing below the midpoint of body 1. When the doji's shadows also gap clear of both neighbors, the pattern becomes the rarer bearish abandoned baby.
failure_modes: Strict gap requirements make genuine instances rare in forex and crypto, and relaxed matches are much less reliable. Strong uptrends often shrug off the pattern after one down candle.
misconceptions: It is not the same as a plain evening star; the star must be a doji. Nor is it a bearish abandoned baby, which additionally requires the doji's full shadow range to be separated by gaps from both neighbors.
example: A stock rallies with a long white candle (80.00 to 83.00), gaps up into a doji near 83.40, then prints a long black candle closing at 80.80. The evening doji star is read as a strong top reversal signal.

name: Three white soldiers
definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long white candles with progressively higher closes, each closing at or near its high and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained buying marking a bottom after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
intuition: Three sessions in a row of determined buying, each marching higher and finishing near its highs, suggests the market has been taken over by confident bulls rather than one-day short covering.
mechanics: From OHLC data: three long white bodies with C1 < C2 < C3; each candle opens within the previous body (no big gaps) and closes near its high (small upper shadows). Appearing after a downtrend or at support, the pattern's steady structure is meant to distinguish genuine accumulation from a spike.
failure_modes: After three strong up candles the market is often short-term overbought, so the pattern frequently completes right before a pullback; late entry is a common way it 'fails'. Very large first or third candles can also signal exhaustion rather than sustained demand.
misconceptions: It is not a signal to chase price higher indefinitely; many practitioners use it to time entries on the ensuing retracement rather than buying the third candle's close. Gapped, non-overlapping opens do not form the classic pattern.
example: After a slide to 45.00, a stock prints three consecutive daily candles closing at 46.20, 47.40, and 48.60, each opening inside the prior body and closing near its high. Chartists read the three white soldiers as evidence of a durable bottom.

name: Three black crows
definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long black candles with progressively lower closes, each closing at or near its low and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained selling marking a top after an advance; it is the bearish mirror of three white soldiers.
intuition: Three sessions in a row of relentless selling, each closing near its lows and stepping lower, suggests determined distribution rather than a single day of profit-taking.
mechanics: From OHLC data: three long black bodies with C1 > C2 > C3; each candle opens within the previous body and closes near its low (small lower shadows). Appearing after an uptrend or at resistance, the stepped structure is meant to distinguish sustained selling from a one-day flush.
failure_modes: After three strong down candles the market is often short-term oversold and due for a bounce, so the pattern frequently completes just before a rebound. Shallow or gapped candles that do not meet the stepped structure are weaker and fail more often.
misconceptions: It is not a signal to short aggressively after completion; the move it 'predicts' has often already happened, so practitioners typically wait for a pullback to enter. Candles with long lower shadows (buying support) do not form a textbook three black crows.
example: After a rally to 95.00, a stock prints three consecutive daily candles closing at 93.50, 92.00, and 90.50, each opening inside the prior body and closing near its low. The three black crows are read as evidence of a durable top.

name: Harami
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small real body is completely contained within the prior session's large real body (the reverse of an engulfing pattern); 'harami' is Japanese for 'pregnant'. Read generically, it marks a sudden loss of momentum in the prevailing trend and is treated in technical analysis as a potential reversal warning, directional (bullish or bearish) according to the trend it interrupts.
intuition: After a big, confident candle, the market suddenly shrinks to a small candle that fits entirely inside the prior body, as if the trend caught its breath and participants hesitated.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 has a large real body; candle 2's open and close both fall strictly inside candle 1's open-close range. Bullish harami: large black body then small body after a decline. Bearish harami: large white body then small body after an advance. If candle 2 is a doji, the pattern is a harami cross.
formula: Harami when min(O2, C2) > min(O1, C1) and max(O2, C2) < max(O1, C1), with body 1 large relative to recent candles.
failure_modes: Harami are frequent and low-powered: many are followed by trend continuation, making them one of the weaker reversal families without confirmation. In tight ranges they occur constantly and mean little.
misconceptions: A harami compares real bodies, not full ranges; a small candle inside the prior candle's full high-low range but not inside its body is an inside bar, a related but distinct concept. It is also a warning of stalling momentum, not a confirmed reversal.
example: In an uptrend, a stock prints a long white candle (50.00 to 53.00), then a small candle that opens at 52.20 and closes at 51.80, entirely inside the prior body. The harami warns that upside momentum has stalled pending the next candle's direction.

name: Bullish harami
definition: A two-candlestick pattern appearing after a downtrend: an unusually large black body is followed by a small white body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bullish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as selling pressure drying up; confirmation from subsequent candles is normally required.
intuition: After a big down day, the market can only manage a tiny up day hidden inside the prior body, suggesting sellers have run out of ammunition and buyers are quietly testing the water.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 is a small white body with both open and close inside body 1's open-close range. The smaller the second body relative to the first, the more pronounced the conventional signal; a doji second candle makes it a (bullish) harami cross.
failure_modes: As a mild two-candle formation it fails often in strong downtrends, where the small candle is merely a pause before new lows. CandleScanner-style statistics show only moderate predictive efficiency even with confirmation.
misconceptions: It is not a strong standalone buy signal; practitioners treat it as a warning and typically require the market to break above the first candle's body. The second candle's shadows may protrude beyond body 1; only the body must be contained.
example: In a downtrend, a stock prints a long black candle (40.00 to 37.00), then a small white candle opening at 37.50 and closing at 38.20. A close above 40.00 within the next sessions would confirm the bullish harami as a three inside up.

name: Bearish harami
definition: A two-candlestick pattern appearing after an uptrend: an unusually large white body is followed by a small black body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as buying pressure drying up; it is the bearish mirror of the bullish harami and requires confirmation.
intuition: After a big up day, the market stalls into a tiny down day nested inside the prior body, suggesting the rally's energy is spent and sellers are probing.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candle 2 is a small black body with both open and close inside body 1's open-close range. A doji second candle turns it into a (bearish) harami cross; a third candle closing below body 1 converts it into the three inside down confirmation pattern.
failure_modes: In persistent uptrends the small contained candle is usually just consolidation, and the trend resumes higher. Its low standalone reliability means unconfirmed bearish harami shorts fail frequently.
misconceptions: It is not a confirmed top; the conventional use waits for price to break below the first candle's body. Only the second candle's body must be contained, not its shadows.
example: In an uptrend, a stock prints a long white candle (65.00 to 68.00), then a small black candle opening at 67.60 and closing at 67.10. Bears treat a subsequent close below 65.00 (a three inside down) as confirmation of the reversal warning.

name: Harami cross
definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a large real body is followed by a doji contained entirely within that body, forming a harami whose second candle is a doji. Technical analysts regard it as a more potent reversal warning than a plain harami because the doji shows the trend's momentum has stalled into outright indecision; it is bullish after declines and bearish after advances.
intuition: A big confident candle is followed by a session that goes absolutely nowhere and hides inside the prior body, suggesting the driving force behind the trend has abruptly evaporated.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 has a large body; candle 2 is a doji (open approximately equal to close) whose body lies inside body 1. Bullish harami cross: large black body then doji after a downtrend. Bearish harami cross: large white body then doji after an uptrend. Confirmation comes from the next candle's direction.
failure_modes: Doji are common, so harami crosses appear often in directionless markets where they carry no reversal information. Even after trends, many instances resolve as continuation once the indecision breaks the prior way.
misconceptions: It is not the same as a doji star (morning/evening doji star): there the doji gaps away from the first body, while here it sits inside it. The second candle must be a true near-zero-body doji, not merely a small candle.
example: After a decline, a stock prints a long black candle (30.00 to 27.00), then a doji opening at 28.10 and closing at 28.12, inside the prior body. The bullish harami cross warns of a possible bottom, pending an up close the next session.

name: Tweezer top
definition: A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose highs match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price ceiling, typically appearing in an uptrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same high as a minor bearish reversal signal, which gains weight when the candles themselves form other reversal shapes.
intuition: The market probed the exact same ceiling twice and failed both times, as if pinched by tweezers at that price, suggesting sellers are defending that level.
mechanics: From OHLC data: two or more candles (consecutive or separated) share essentially equal highs; the first is typically a white candle and the second a black candle in the classic uptrend form. The matching highs define an ad-hoc resistance level whose subsequent break invalidates the bearish reading.
failure_modes: Matching highs occur constantly by chance, so isolated tweezer tops have low standalone significance. In strong uptrends the double test often precedes a breakout rather than a reversal.
misconceptions: The candles do not have to be adjacent, and their bodies can be any size; what matters is the matching highs. It is a minor signal on its own, not a major reversal pattern like an evening star.
example: A stock rallies and prints a white candle with a high of 77.00, then the next session trades up to 77.00 again but closes lower as a black candle. The tweezer top marks 77.00 as resistance and warns of a possible pullback.

name: Tweezer bottom
definition: A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose lows match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price floor, typically appearing in a downtrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same low as a minor bullish reversal signal, the mirror of the tweezer top, which gains weight when combined with other reversal shapes.
intuition: The market probed the exact same floor twice and held both times, as if supported by tweezers at that price, suggesting buyers are defending that level.
mechanics: From OHLC data: two or more candles (consecutive or separated) share essentially equal lows; the first is typically a black candle and the second a white candle in the classic downtrend form. The matching lows define an ad-hoc support level whose break invalidates the bullish reading.
failure_modes: Matching lows are common by coincidence, so isolated tweezer bottoms carry little weight. In strong downtrends the double bottom at the lows often gives way to further declines.
misconceptions: The candles need not be adjacent or similar in size; only the lows must match. It is a minor confirmation-level signal, not a major standalone reversal pattern.
example: A stock falls and prints a black candle with a low of 22.00, then the next session dips to 22.00 again before closing higher as a white candle. The tweezer bottom marks 22.00 as support and hints at a possible bounce.

name: Three inside up
definition: A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish harami: a long black body in a downtrend is followed by a small white body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami.
intuition: First the trend's selling stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes higher, confirming that buyers, not sellers, won the standoff.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 is a white (non-doji) body engulfed by body 1; candle 3 closes above candle 2's close (many implementations require a white body). Shadow lengths are disregarded. Practitioners often seek further confirmation via a break of nearby resistance or a trendline.
formula: Three inside up when C1 < O1 (long body), O1 > O2, C2 > C1, min(O2, C2) > C1, max(O2, C2) < O1, and C3 > C2.
failure_modes: Backtested occurrence statistics show only moderate efficiency; many instances fail in strong downtrends despite the built-in confirmation. Signals forming far from support or on low volume underperform.
misconceptions: It is not just 'any three rising candles'; the first two must form a genuine bullish harami with body containment. It is also a Morris-era formalization, not one of the classical Japanese patterns.
example: After a decline, a stock prints a long black candle (50.00 to 47.00), a small white candle inside it (47.50 to 48.30), then a third candle closing at 48.90, above the second close. The three inside up confirms the harami as a bullish reversal signal.

name: Three inside down
definition: A three-candlestick bearish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bearish harami: a long white body in an uptrend is followed by a small black body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing below the second candle's close. The third candle's lower close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami.
intuition: First the rally stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes lower, confirming that sellers, not buyers, won the standoff.

Shadow lengths are disregarded; a close of candle 3 below candle 1's close is considered stronger confirmation.
formula: Three inside down when C1 > O1 (long body), O2 < C1, C2 > O1, min(O2, C2) > O1, max(O2, C2) < C1, and C3 < C2.
failure_modes: Even with the built-in confirmation, many instances fail in strong uptrends where the dip is immediately bought. Empirical frequency-efficiency statistics (e.g., CandleScanner on S&P 500 data) show only moderate predictive power.
misconceptions: It is not any three declining candles; the first two must form a genuine bearish harami with the second body inside the first. It is a modern formalization by Morris, not a classical Japanese pattern.
example: After a rally, a stock prints a long white candle (60.00 to 63.00), a small black candle inside it (62.50 to 61.70), then a third candle closing at 61.20, below the second close. The three inside down confirms the harami as a bearish reversal signal.

name: Three outside up
definition: A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish engulfing: a black body in a downtrend is engulfed by a larger white body (the engulfing), and then a third white candle closes above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close confirms the engulfing signal.
intuition: Buyers first swallow the prior down candle whole, then prove it was no fluke by closing higher again the very next session.

formula: Three outside up when C1 < O1, O2 <= C1, C2 >= O1, C2 > O2, and C3 > C2 (with candle 3 white).
failure_modes: Despite the extra confirmation candle, the pattern still fails regularly in persistent downtrends; published S&P 500 scan statistics show a substantial share of false signals. Late entry after the third candle can leave a poor risk-reward location.
misconceptions: It is not a synonym for bullish engulfing; it is the engulfing plus a confirming third candle. It is also a modern Morris construction rather than a classical Japanese pattern.
example: In a downtrend, a stock prints a black candle (45.00 to 43.50), a long white candle engulfing it (43.20 to 45.50), then a third white candle closing at 46.10. The three outside up is read as a confirmed bullish reversal.

name: Rising three methods
definition: A five-candlestick bullish continuation pattern: a long white body is followed by three small bodies (normally black) that all remain within the first candle's range, and then a final long white body closing above the first candle's close. Technical analysts read it as a brief, contained pause within an ongoing advance; it is a continuation, not reversal, formation.
intuition: The market surges, then drifts sideways-to-down for three small sessions without giving back the surge, then surges again, showing the pullback was only profit-taking inside a healthy uptrend.
mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candles 2-4 are small bodies (typically black) whose highs and lows stay inside candle 1's range; candle 5 is a long white body closing above candle 1's close. The containment of the middle candles within the first candle's range is the defining test.
failure_modes: It is rare in its strict form, and relaxed matches (middle candles escaping the first candle's range) are much less reliable. If the fifth candle fails to exceed the first candle's close, the supposed continuation often reverses instead.
misconceptions: The middle three candles must stay inside the first candle's range; three strong down candles that break below it are not a 'rising' anything. It is also a continuation pattern: looking for it as a bottom reversal misapplies the concept.
example: A stock jumps with a long white candle (50.00 to 53.00), then prints three small black candles between 52.90 and 51.20, then a long white candle closing at 54.10. The rising three methods is read as the uptrend pausing, then resuming.

name: Falling three methods

It is the bearish mirror of rising three methods, read as a contained pause within an ongoing decline.

Containment of the middle candles within the first candle's range is the defining test.

example: A stock drops with a long black candle (60.00 to 57.00), then prints three small white candles between 57.20 and 58.80, then a long black candle closing at 55.90. The falling three methods is read as the downtrend pausing, then resuming.

name: Abandoned baby
definition: A rare three-candlestick reversal pattern similar to a morning/evening doji star but stricter: the middle doji must gap away from both neighboring candles such that its shadows do not overlap theirs at either side. The bullish version (doji gapped below between a black and a white candle) and bearish version (doji gapped above between a white and a black candle) are read as major reversal signals.
intuition: A lone doji sits isolated on the chart with empty space on both sides, like an abandoned baby; the market gapped away from the trend, froze, and then gapped back the opposite way.
mechanics: Bullish form: long black candle, then a doji whose high is below the prior candle's low, then a white candle whose low is above the doji's high. Bearish form mirrors this with gaps above. Because it requires two full shadow gaps around a doji, it is extremely rare: multi-decade S&P 500 scans find only a handful of occurrences.
formula: Bullish abandoned baby when H2 < L1 (doji = candle 2) and L3 > H2; bearish when L2 > H1 and H3 < L2.
failure_modes: Its rarity makes it almost unusable in practice and prevents meaningful statistical validation; tiny samples give unreliable efficiency estimates. In gapless 24-hour markets genuine instances are nearly nonexistent, and relaxed matches degrade into ordinary doji stars.
misconceptions: It is not just a morning or evening doji star: the doji's entire shadow range must be separated by gaps from both neighbors, not merely its body. Its textbook rarity also means most chart 'sightings' do not meet the strict definition.
example: A stock in a downtrend prints a long black candle (low 28.00), then a doji trading entirely between 27.20 and 27.60, then a white candle whose low is 27.80 and which closes at 29.50. The fully gapped doji makes this a bullish abandoned baby rather than a morning doji star.

name: Kicker pattern
definition: A two-candlestick reversal pattern consisting of two opposite-colored marubozu-type candles: the first moves with the prevailing trend, and the second gaps open at or beyond the first candle's open and drives in the opposite direction, nullifying it. Technical analysts regard it as one of the strongest reversal formations, typically attributed to a sudden news-driven shift in sentiment.
intuition: The market is moving firmly one way, then overnight something changes so completely that price gaps to the other side of the prior open and runs the opposite way all session, kicking the trend into reverse.
mechanics: Bullish kicker: black candle (close near its low) in a downtrend, then a white candle that gaps up to open at or above the first candle's open and closes near its high, with no overlap of the two real bodies. Bearish kicker mirrors this. The gap plus zero body overlap is the defining feature; the gap is usually driven by a news event.
formula: Bullish kicker when C1 < O1, O2 >= O1, C2 > O2, and the bodies do not overlap; bearish kicker mirrors with C1 > O1, O2 <= O1, C2 < O2.
failure_modes: In markets that rarely gap (spot forex, 24-hour crypto) genuine kickers almost never occur. Even in equities, a news-driven gap can be fully faded in the following sessions, so the 'strongest reversal' reputation does not make it reliable without context.
misconceptions: It is not an engulfing pattern: the second candle opens beyond the first candle's open via a gap, rather than engulfing the body from within. The two candles also conventionally show little or no shadows (marubozu-like).
example: A stock slides, closing near its low at 32.00 after opening at 34.00. Overnight, positive earnings news gaps it up to open at 34.10, and it rallies to close near its high at 36.50. The bullish kicker is read as an abrupt sentiment reversal.

name: Inside bar
definition: A bar whose entire high-low range is contained within the range of the preceding bar (the 'mother bar'): its high is at or below the prior high and its low is at or above the prior low. Price-action traders read it as volatility compression and indecision, traded as a breakout setup in either direction rather than as an inherently bullish or bearish signal.
intuition: The market took a breath: the latest bar traded entirely inside the previous bar's range, coiling like a spring while buy and sell stop orders pile up on both sides of the mother bar.
mechanics: From OHLC data: High_t < High_{t-1} and Low_t > Low_{t-1} (strict; some conventions allow equality). The body color is irrelevant. Common usage places stop orders beyond the mother bar's high and low and treats the triggered side as a continuation or reversal entry depending on context.
formula: Inside bar when H_t < H_{t-1} and L_t > L_{t-1} (strict form).
failure_modes: On low timeframes inside bars form constantly and produce many false breakouts; whipsaws around the mother bar's extremes are common in choppy markets. The pattern gives no directional edge by itself, so breakout entries fail roughly as often as they succeed without trend or level confluence.
misconceptions: An inside bar is not inherently bullish or bearish, and it is not the same as a harami: the harami compares real bodies, while the inside bar compares full high-low ranges. A doji whose shadows exceed the mother bar is not an inside bar.
example: A daily bar trades between 100 and 104; the next bar trades only between 101 and 103. A trader places a buy stop at 104.10 and a sell stop at 99.90, letting the market's break of the mother bar's range decide the trade direction.

name: Outside bar
definition: A bar whose high exceeds the prior bar's high and whose low falls below the prior bar's low, so its full range engulfs the previous bar's range. Price-action traders read it as volatility expansion and a battle between buyers and sellers, with the close's location indicating which side won; it differs from the engulfing candlestick pattern, which compares only real bodies.
intuition: The market explored beyond both edges of the previous session in one bar, a burst of expanded volatility where both sides were tested and the close reveals the winner.
mechanics: From OHLC data: High_t > High_{t-1} and Low_t < Low_{t-1}. The close near the high is read bullishly and near the low bearishly, especially at support/resistance; a mid-range close is considered weak. Its wide range makes stop placement and position sizing a central practical issue.
formula: Outside bar when H_t > H_{t-1} and L_t < L_{t-1}.
failure_modes: The wide range forces wide stops, so a single failed trade is expensive; mid-range closes are especially prone to whipsaw. In trendless chop, outside bars frequently mark two-sided stop-runs rather than genuine reversals or continuations.
misconceptions: An outside bar is not identical to an engulfing pattern: engulfing requires only the real body to be engulfed, while the outside bar requires the entire shadow range to be engulfed. Nor is every outside bar a reversal signal; many act as continuation bars within trends.
example: After an uptrend stalls at resistance, a bar trades from a low of 47.50 to a high of 50.50, fully outside the prior bar's 48.00-50.00 range, and closes at 47.80 near its low. Traders read this bearish outside bar as supply overwhelming demand at resistance.

name: Pin bar
definition: A single-candlestick price-action pattern with a small real body and one very long shadow protruding in one direction, the name deriving from Martin Pring's 'Pinocchio bar' because the long wick 'lies' about market direction by showing a rejected probe. Traders read the long shadow as rejection of a price level and use it as a reversal or continuation trigger, typically in confluence with support and resistance.
intuition: Price made a quick dash far in one direction and was slapped back before the close, leaving a long nose; the dash is treated as a lie that reveals where the market refuses to go.
mechanics: From OHLC data: a common heuristic requires the dominant shadow to be at least two-thirds of the bar's total range, with the small body at the opposite end; body color is secondary. In strict price-action usage the bar only 'counts' as a tradeable pin bar when its wick penetrates a meaningful support/resistance level and closes back on the other side, trapping breakout traders.
formula: Bearish pin bar heuristic: (H - max(O, C)) >= (2/3) * (H - L); bullish pin bar: (min(O, C) - L) >= (2/3) * (H - L).
failure_modes: Pin-shaped bars occur constantly on all timeframes, so most are noise; without a key level or trend context the pattern has little edge. Failed pin bars are common enough that some traders specifically trade the failures, and the wide stop beyond the wick can produce poor risk-reward.
misconceptions: A pin bar is not defined by shape alone in rigorous usage; the same bar is a hammer, hanging man, shooting star, or inverted hammer in classical candlestick taxonomy, with context determining the label. It is also not a standalone strategy: practitioners emphasize that context and confirmation matter more than the bar's geometry.
example: EUR/USD pokes above a well-watched 1.1000 resistance to 1.1040 intraday but closes back at 1.0985, leaving a long upper wick. Price-action traders read the bearish pin bar as a rejected breakout and consider shorts below the bar's low with a stop above 1.1040.
